findings.title: Comment inaccurately describes error handling behavior
findings.body: The added comment suggests the function checks upstream availability, but `fetch(url)` throws on network/DNS errors and is not wrapped in a try/catch. When the upstream is genuinely unavailable, the caller gets an unhandled rejection instead of `false`. Wrap the `fetch` call in a try/catch block that returns `false` on failure to align behavior with the documented intent.

findings.title: Concurrent-call deduplication removed, causing thundering herd
findings.body: The original `pending` map ensured that overlapping calls to `loadCached` with the same key shared a single in-flight `fetchValue()` call. The new code removes that mechanism, so every concurrent call will separately await `fetchValue()` for the same key. This regresses both performance (duplicate I/O) and potentially correctness if `fetchValue` has side effects. Restore a per-key promise cache, or at minimum document the changed contract.

While harmless, it obscures the control flow. Remove the condition or keep it only if the code between lines 7 and 9 could have inserted a value (it cannot).

findings.title: Loss of request deduplication for concurrent calls

findings.title: Concurrent `fetchValue` calls for the same key after removing deduplication
findings.body: The old code used a `pending` map so that if `loadCached` was called concurrently with the same key, only one `fetchValue` would run and all callers would share its promise. This means `fetchValue` may be invoked multiple times for the same key, wasting work and potentially causing duplicate side effects. Restore the deduplication pattern or document that callers must serialize calls externally.

findings.title: Race condition: concurrent requests for the same key bypass deduplication
findings.body: The original `pending` Map ensured that if two callers invoke `loadCached(k, f)` before `f()` resolves, only one call to `fetchValue()` is made and both callers await the same promise. The new code removes this protection. Two concurrent callers will both see `cache.has(key) === false`, both call `fetchValue()`, and the second caller's result overwrites the first's cache entry. This wastes work, can trigger expensive or side-effectful fetches multiple times, and creates a window where cache state is inconsistent. To fix, restore the deduplication pattern or use a per-key promise map.

findings.title: Redundant guard after cache-miss check
findings.body: The function returned early on line 7 when `cache.get(key)` returned a value, so by line 10 we already know `cache.has(key) === false`. The `if (!cache.has(key))` is dead code; it always evaluates to `true`. This adds no protection and misleads readers. Either remove the guard or restructure the function into a single cache-miss branch.

findings.title: Unnecessary non-null assertion when local variable holds the value
findings.body: The function already holds `value` from the `await fetchValue()` on line 11. It can return `value` directly instead of performing a second `Map#get` lookup and masking the result with a non-null assertion. If `fetchValue()` throws, execution never reaches this line, so the `!` is technically safe but needlessly hides the type relationship and adds a redundant map read.

findings.title: Always returns true regardless of HTTP response status
findings.body: The function previously returned `response.ok`, which reflected whether the HTTP request succeeded. Now it unconditionally returns `true`, so every caller will believe the fetch succeeded even when the server returns 4xx/5xx or the network is unreachable. Either maintain the original return (which is the documented contract) or, if fire-and-forget is truly intended, remove the return value and update the function signature.

findings.title: Fire-and-forget fetch creates unhandled promise rejection risk
findings.body: `void fetch(url)` discards the promise. If the network request rejects (e.g. DNS failure, timeout, CORS error), Node.js will emit an `unhandledRejection` and may crash the process; browsers will log a noisy warning. The old code at least allowed the rejection to propagate to the caller. Add a `.catch()` handler if the fire-and-forget pattern is desired, or restore the await.

findings.body: The original `applyEdit` used `if (!canEdit(doc, userId))` to block unauthorized users. The extracted `assertEditable` at line 32 omits the `!` negation, so it now throws when the user **can** edit — the exact inverse of the intended behavior. This lets unauthorized users (viewers or non-members) edit documents while blocking owners and editors. Add back the `!` to make it `if (!canEdit(doc, userId))`.
